tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 62-year-old man with chronic kidney disease stage 4 (baseline GFR 22) on maintenance hemodialysis presents after missing his last two dialysis sessions due to transportation issues. He reports 2 days of progressive generalized weakness, muscle cramps, and palpitations. He has continued to eat his usual diet, including bananas and orange juice. On examination, he appears fatigued and mildly short of breath. Vital signs: T 36.6C, HR 52 (irregular), RR 20, BP 172/96, SpO2 95%. Lower extremity exam reveals 2+ bilateral pitting edema and diminished deep tendon reflexes. Labs: potassium 7.8 mEq/L, BUN 112 mg/dL, creatinine 11.4 mg/dL, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, phosphorus 8.2 mg/dL. ECG demonstrates absent P waves, widened QRS complexes (duration 180 ms), and peaked T waves with a sine wave pattern beginning to emerge. IV calcium gluconate is administered emergently.
winner_protocol:
Age: 62
Sex: Male
Complaint: 2 days of progressive generalized weakness, muscle cramps, and palpitations in a hemodialysis-dependent patient who missed two consecutive dialysis sessions.

Analysis: This is a life-threatening presentation of severe hyperkalemia (K+ 7.8 mEq/L) in a CKD stage 4 patient on maintenance hemodialysis who missed two sessions. The ECG findings — absent P waves, widened QRS complexes (180 ms), peaked T waves with an emerging sine wave pattern — are hallmark signs of severe hyperkalemia with impending cardiac arrest. Bradycardia (HR 52, irregular) and diminished deep tendon reflexes further support the diagnosis. Contributing factors include missed dialysis sessions, continued dietary potassium intake (bananas, orange juice), metabolic acidosis (HCO3- 14), and worsening uremia (BUN 112, Cr 11.4). Volume overload is evidenced by 2+ pitting edema and hypertension (172/96). Hyperphosphatemia (8.2 mg/dL) is also present from renal failure. IV calcium gluconate has already been administered emergently to stabilize the cardiac membrane. The main differential considerations include other causes of bradycardia and widened QRS, but hyperkalemia clearly explains all findings. Adrenal insufficiency is less likely given the hypertension. No medications are mentioned that would suggest drug-induced hyperkalemia.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous cardiac monitoring; serial serum potassium measurements; repeat ECG after each intervention; arterial or venous blood gas for acid-base assessment.

Conclusion: Life-threatening hyperkalemia (K+ 7.8 mEq/L) with severe ECG changes in a dialysis-dependent patient who missed two hemodialysis sessions, complicated by metabolic acidosis, uremia, hyperphosphatemia, and volume overload. Emergent hemodialysis is the definitive treatment; all other interventions are temporizing.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Nephrology

Recommendations: 1. Maintain continuous cardiac monitoring; prepare for potential arrhythmia management including defibrillation if ventricular fibrillation occurs. 2. Repeat IV calcium gluconate if ECG changes persist or recur after initial dose. 3. Administer IV regular insulin (10 units) with 50% dextrose (25 g) to shift potassium intracellularly. 4. Consider nebulized albuterol (10–20 mg) for additional intracellular potassium shift. 5. Administer IV sodium bicarbonate to correct metabolic acidosis and further reduce serum potassium. 6. Arrange emergent hemodialysis as the definitive treatment — ensure vascular access is confirmed and ready; do not delay. 7. Admit to ICU for close monitoring during and after dialysis. 8. Start phosphate binders for hyperphosphatemia after initial stabilization. 9. Address the root cause: arrange reliable transportation services to prevent future missed dialysis sessions. 10. Provide dietary counseling on potassium restriction, including avoidance of bananas, orange juice, and other high-potassium foods.

Notes: The emerging sine wave pattern on ECG indicates imminent risk of ventricular fibrillation or asystole. IV calcium gluconate has already been administered per the case. All pharmacological interventions except hemodialysis are temporizing measures only; emergent dialysis is the definitive treatment and must not be delayed.

Vignette: A 15-year-old girl presents with her mother for evaluation of bumps on her forehead and chin that have been present for the past 3 months. She reports they are not painful but she finds them cosmetically bothersome. She has been washing her face with regular soap twice daily. She denies any cystic lesions, scarring, or use of new cosmetics. Menarche was 1 year ago and her cycles are regular. She takes no medications. On examination, there are scattered open and closed comedones on the forehead and chin numbering approximately 15 to 20. A few small inflammatory papules, each less than 5 mm, are noted on the chin. There are no nodules, cysts, or scarring.
Simplified (added symptoms): 15 y/o f, scattered comedones and few small papules on forehead and chin x3 mo, ~15-20 lesions, no cysts, nodules, or scarring, cosmetically bothersome

She reports they are not painful but she finds them cosmetically bothersome. She has been washing her face with regular soap twice daily. Age: 52
Sex: Male
Complaint: Polyuria, polydipsia, unintentional weight loss (10 pounds over 2 months), blurry vision, and increased fatigue over several weeks
Analysis: The patient presents with classic hyperglycemic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, blurry vision, fatigue) strongly suggestive of new-onset diabetes mellitus. Multiple risk factors support type 2 diabetes: obesity (BMI 36), family history in both parents, sedentary lifestyle, and acanthosis nigricans on physical examination (a hallmark of insulin resistance). Laboratory confirmation is definitive: fasting plasma glucose of 210 mg/dL exceeds the diagnostic threshold of 126 mg/dL, and HbA1c of 9.2% exceeds the diagnostic threshold of 6.5%. The absence of ketonuria effectively excludes diabetic ketoacidosis. Differential considerations include type 1 diabetes/LADA, but the clinical picture (obesity, acanthosis nigricans, strong family history of type 2 diabetes) overwhelmingly favors type 2 diabetes. Hypertension is suboptimally controlled at 144/92 mmHg despite lisinopril, requiring medication adjustment. Hyperlipidemia history necessitates baseline lipid evaluation and statin therapy consideration per diabetic guidelines.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Comprehensive metabolic panel (renal function, liver function), fasting lipid panel, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, comprehensive ophthalmologic examination, ECG

Subclinical specialization: General Medicine

2. Lifestyle modifications: structured diabetic diet plan, weight loss goal of 5-10% body weight, gradual exercise program starting with daily walking.
3. Adjust antihypertensive therapy — target blood pressure <130/80 mmHg; uptitrate lisinopril or add a second agent such as amlodipine or thiazide diuretic.

8. Obtain urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio for nephropathy screening.

winner_protocol:
Age: 52
Sex: Female
Complaint: 3-month history of progressively worsening deep, aching left shoulder pain and stiffness, worse at night, with difficulty performing overhead and behind-the-back activities; no preceding trauma.
Analysis: The clinical picture is most consistent with primary adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder). The strongest supporting facts are the globally restricted active and passive range of motion (external rotation limited to 20°, abduction to 80°, severe internal rotation restriction), the absence of preceding trauma, the absence of focal rotator cuff tenderness, and radiographs excluding fracture, dislocation, or significant osteoarthritis. Type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 7.8%) is a well-established predisposing risk factor for adhesive capsulitis. Key differential considerations include rotator cuff tear (typically preserves passive ROM and shows focal tendon tenderness or true weakness), subacromial impingement (painful arc, passive ROM preserved), glenohumeral osteoarthritis (radiographic joint space narrowing and osteophytes, which are absent here), and cervical radiculopathy (associated with distal radicular symptoms and neurologic deficits, not described here). The globally restricted passive ROM is the critical distinguishing feature favoring adhesive capsulitis over these alternatives.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Primary adhesive capsulitis of the left shoulder in a 52-year-old diabetic woman, supported by globally restricted active and passive ROM and unremarkable radiographs. Diabetes is a contributing risk factor and glycemic control is suboptimal.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Initiate conservative management with analgesia (e.g., oral NSAIDs if not contraindicated) and a structured physical therapy program emphasizing gentle progressive stretching and mobilization of the glenohumeral joint. Consider referral to orthopedics for evaluation of an intra-articular corticosteroid injection, particularly given persistent night pain and functional limitation. Address diabetes optimization with the patient's endocrinology or primary care provider, as elevated HbA1c (7.8%) may prolong recovery and increase recurrence risk. Reassess in 4–6 weeks; if no improvement, consider MRI to evaluate for occult rotator cuff pathology and formal orthopedic referral.
Notes: Intra-articular corticosteroid injection may transiently elevate blood glucose; diabetic patients should be counseled to monitor glucose more closely for several days after injection.

Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.

The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.

- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case

The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol

criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

[6]
tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

winner_protocol:
Age: 40
Sex: Male
Complaint: 10-day worsening facial pressure, purulent nasal discharge, congestion, anosmia, postnasal drip, and nocturnal productive cough in context of chronic rhinosinusitis with bilateral nasal polyps and recurrent sinus infections (4-5 per year) with prior polypectomy.
Analysis: This presentation is consistent with an acute bacterial exacerbation of chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP). Supporting facts include: 10-day worsening symptoms with purulent discharge and sinus tenderness (bacterial rather than viral pattern), visible polypoid tissue with mucopurulent drainage in the middle meatus, cobblestoning of the posterior pharyngeal wall indicating chronic postnasal drainage, and a history of recurrent infections and prior polypectomy suggesting persistent mucosal inflammation and possible polyp regrowth. Absence of fever, visual changes, or severe headache makes complications (orbital cellulitis, intracranial extension) unlikely. From an allergist/immunologist perspective, recurrent CRSwNP with frequent exacerbations warrants evaluation for allergic and environmental contributors (e.g., dust mite, mold, pet dander, pollens, secondhand smoke) that may be driving chronic type 2 inflammation and polyp recurrence. The nighttime cough may reflect postnasal drainage but could also indicate lower airway involvement (asthma or eosinophilic bronchitis), which should be considered given the association between CRSwNP and airway eosinophilia.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Nasal endoscopy; CT of paranasal sinuses (if not recently performed) to assess polyp extent and ostiomeatal complex obstruction; skin prick testing or specific IgE testing to common inhalant allergens; complete blood count with differential to assess eosinophilia; total serum IgE; consideration of nasal swab/culture for targeted antibiotic therapy if purulence persists.
Conclusion: Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis superimposed on chronic rhinosinusitis with bilateral nasal polyps and recurrent infections, likely with underlying allergic or eosinophilic inflammatory contribution requiring both acute antimicrobial management and long-term anti-inflammatory and allergen-trigger evaluation.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)
Recommendations: Initiate antibiotic therapy targeting typical sinus pathogens (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanate or doxycycline) for 10-14 days. Start or optimize intranasal corticosteroid therapy; consider a short course of oral corticosteroids for polyp-associated inflammation. Recommend saline nasal irrigation. Conduct a detailed environmental exposure history (tobacco smoke, indoor allergens, seasonal exposures) and proceed with skin or specific IgE testing to identify sensitization. If allergen sensitization is confirmed and thought to drive persistent symptoms, counsel on allergen avoidance/remediation and consider subcutaneous or sublingual immunotherapy. Schedule ENT follow-up to assess need for revision polypectomy or biologic therapy (e.g., dupilumab) if medical therapy fails. Advise the patient to return immediately if fever, visual changes, or severe headache develop.
Notes: Recurrent polyps after prior surgery suggest ongoing inflammation that may benefit from long-term anti-inflammatory and allergy-directed treatment; lower airway symptoms (nocturnal cough) should prompt evaluation for coexisting asthma.

tags: ['axis:accuracy']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

[3]
tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

[5]
tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

[6]
tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 35-year-old male teacher presents with 2 days of nasal congestion, frequent sneezing, mild sore throat, and a low-grade temperature of 37.6°C. He reports several students in his classroom have been out sick recently. He notes mild fatigue but denies cough, dyspnea, myalgias, or ear pain. On examination, the nasal turbinates are mildly swollen with clear discharge. The oropharynx is mildly erythematous without tonsillar enlargement or exudates. Tympanic membranes are clear. Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. He is well-hydrated and in no acute distress.
winner_protocol:
Age: 35
Sex: Male
Complaint: 2 days of nasal congestion, frequent sneezing, mild sore throat, and low-grade fever (37.6°C), with mild fatigue.
Analysis: The presentation is most consistent with an uncomplicated viral upper respiratory infection. Supporting facts include short symptom duration (2 days), clear nasal discharge with swollen turbinates, low-grade fever, mild oropharyngeal erythema without tonsillar exudate or enlargement, and sick contacts in the classroom. The absence of cough, myalgias, and high fever makes influenza less likely. No tonsillar exudate or cervical adenopathy and only low-grade fever place streptococcal pharyngitis low on the differential (Centor criteria approximately 0–1). No facial pressure or purulent discharge argues against acute bacterial rhinosinusitis. Allergic rhinitis is possible given sneezing and clear discharge, but the fever and sick contacts favor an infectious etiology. Infectious mononucleosis is unlikely given the brief duration and absence of significant fatigue, exudate, or adenopathy. No red flags such as dyspnea, drooling, ear pain, or worsening after initial improvement are present.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Uncomplicated viral upper respiratory infection (common cold). No features suggesting bacterial infection, influenza, or other complications at this time.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine
Recommendations: Symptomatic supportive care is recommended: adequate hydration, rest, saline nasal spray or irrigation for congestion, and over-the-counter analgesics (e.g., acetaminophen or ibuprofen) as needed for sore throat and low-grade fever. Antihistamines or decongestants may be used short-term if symptoms are bothersome. Antibiotics are not indicated. Set expectations that symptoms typically resolve within 7–10 days. Instruct the patient to return if symptoms worsen after initial improvement, if high fever develops, if facial pressure or purulent nasal discharge persists beyond 10 days, if ear pain or dyspnea occurs, or if sore throat significantly worsens with difficulty swallowing or drooling.
Notes: As a teacher with ongoing classroom exposure, reinforce hand hygiene and consider masking if symptoms persist while interacting with students.

Five days ago, he had a lower left second molar extracted at a dental clinic. He has no significant past medical history. criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 35-year-old man presents with 3 days of progressive bilateral submandibular and sublingual swelling, worsening trismus, odynophagia, and a muffled "hot potato" voice. Five days ago, he had a lower left second molar extracted at a dental clinic. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, he is sitting upright and drooling, appearing anxious and in respiratory distress. Vital signs: T 38.8C, HR 114, RR 24, BP 138/82, SpO2 91% on room air. There is firm, woody, bilateral submandibular swelling with erythema and warmth. The floor of the mouth is elevated and indurated, displacing the tongue posteriorly and superiorly. He is unable to fully open his mouth. Inspiratory stridor is audible. CT neck with contrast demonstrates a multiloculated fluid collection in the submandibular and sublingual spaces bilaterally with significant airway narrowing at the level of the oropharynx.
winner_protocol:
Age: 35
Sex: Male
Complaint: Progressive bilateral submandibular and sublingual swelling with trismus, odynophagia, muffled "hot potato" voice, and respiratory distress following recent lower molar dental extraction 5 days prior.

Analysis: This presentation is consistent with Ludwig's angina, a rapidly progressive cellulitis of the submandibular and sublingual spaces. Key supporting facts: recent lower molar extraction (a classic precipitant), firm woody bilateral submandibular swelling with erythema, elevated and indurated floor of mouth displacing the tongue posteriorly and superiorly, "hot potato" voice, trismus, fever (38.8C), tachycardia (HR 114), hypoxia (SpO2 91% on room air), and audible inspiratory stridor indicating impending airway obstruction. CT neck with contrast confirms multiloculated fluid collections in the submandibular and sublingual spaces bilaterally with significant oropharyngeal airway narrowing. Differential considerations include retropharyngeal abscess, parapharyngeal abscess, peritonsillar abscess, epiglottitis, and allergic angioedema; however, the bilateral submandibular involvement, elevated floor of mouth, posterior tongue displacement, and recent dental extraction most strongly support Ludwig's angina. The patient is in imminent danger of complete airway obstruction.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: CT neck with contrast has already been performed and confirms the diagnosis. No additional diagnostic imaging is required. Basic preoperative laboratory studies (CBC, basic metabolic panel, coagulation panel, blood cultures) may be obtained in parallel with airway management but should not delay definitive treatment.

Conclusion: Ludwig's angina secondary to recent dental extraction with impending airway compromise, requiring emergent airway stabilization, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and urgent surgical drainage.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Emergency

Recommendations: 1) Immediate airway management is the top priority — arrange awake fiberoptic nasotracheal intubation by the most experienced operator available; have surgical airway equipment (cricothyrotomy or tracheostomy) at the bedside as backup. 2) Keep the patient sitting upright; do not place supine as this may worsen airway obstruction. 3) Do not attempt blind or rapid sequence intubation without fiberoptic guidance due to distorted anatomy and high risk of complete obstruction. 4) Initiate IV broad-spectrum antibiotics covering oral aerobic and anaerobic flora (e.g., ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin plus ceftriaxone). 5) Urgent consultation with Otolaryngology (ENT) and/or Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery for surgical drainage of the bilateral submandibular and sublingual fluid collections. 6) Admit to ICU post-airway stabilization for continuous airway monitoring and ongoing management.

Notes: This is a life-threatening airway emergency with significant mortality if the airway is not secured promptly. Do not leave the patient unattended. Avoid sedatives or muscle relaxants that could precipitate complete airway loss. Surgical airway equipment must remain at bedside throughout stabilization and transport.

Vignette: A 24-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks gestation is brought in by ambulance after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home lasting approximately 2 minutes. Her partner reports she has complained of a persistent headache, visual disturbances described as flashing lights, and swelling of her face and hands over the past 2 days. She did not attend her last two prenatal appointments. On examination, she is postictal, moaning, and not following commands. Vital signs: T 37.6C, HR 112, RR 22, BP 182/116, SpO2 94%. Significant periorbital and bilateral upper extremity edema is present. Deep tendon reflexes are 4+ bilaterally with sustained clonus at the ankles. Fetal heart rate monitoring shows persistent late decelerations. Labs: platelets 92,000/mcL, AST 286 U/L, ALT 312 U/L, LDH 680 U/L, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 5.2. IV magnesium sulfate is initiated and emergent cesarean delivery is planned.

Vignette:
A 24-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks gestation is brought in by ambulance after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home lasting approximately 2 minutes. Her partner reports she has complained of a persistent headache, visual disturbances described as flashing lights, and swelling of her face and hands over the past 2 days. She did not attend her last two prenatal appointments. On examination, she is postictal, moaning, and not following commands. Vital signs: T 37.6C, HR 112, RR 22, BP 182/116, SpO2 94%. Significant periorbital and bilateral upper extremity edema is present. Deep tendon reflexes are 4+ bilaterally with sustained clonus at the ankles. Fetal heart rate monitoring shows persistent late decelerations. Labs: platelets 92,000/mcL, AST 286 U/L, ALT 312 U/L, LDH 680 U/L, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 5.2. IV magnesium sulfate is initiated and emergent cesarean delivery is planned.
winner_protocol:
Age: 24
Sex: Female
Complaint: Postictal primigravida at 36 weeks gestation with severe hypertension, eclamptic seizure, signs of severe preeclampsia with HELLP features, and fetal distress requiring emergent cesarean delivery.
Analysis: This patient presents with eclampsia complicated by severe preeclampsia features. The diagnosis is supported by: witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure, severe hypertension (182/116), hyperreflexia with sustained clonus, thrombocytopenia (platelets 92,000/mcL), elevated transaminases (AST 286, ALT 312), elevated LDH (680), elevated creatinine (1.4), and marked proteinuria (protein-to-creatinine ratio 5.2). Persistent late fetal decelerations indicate fetal compromise, necessitating emergent cesarean delivery. The platelet count of 92,000/mcL, while above the absolute 50,000 threshold, raises concern for evolving consumptive coagulopathy and HELLP syndrome, which may worsen perioperatively. The postictal state and magnesium sulfate infusion further complicate anesthetic management. Main differential considerations include eclampsia with HELLP syndrome (most likely), underlying seizure disorder (less likely given hypertension, proteinuria, and lab abnormalities), and intracranial hemorrhage (possible given severe hypertension and seizure, though less likely primary). From an anesthetic standpoint, the combination of thrombocytopenia, postictal altered mental status, and hemodynamic instability risk favors rapid sequence induction general anesthesia over neuraxial technique.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Fibrinogen level, PT/INR, aPTT, blood type and screen/crossmatch, arterial line for continuous blood pressure monitoring, point-of-care hemoglobin, additional platelet count trend.
Conclusion: Eclampsia with severe preeclampsia and features of HELLP syndrome at 36 weeks gestation, complicated by fetal distress, requiring emergent cesarean delivery under general anesthesia with rapid sequence induction, massive transfusion preparation, and intensive hemodynamic monitoring.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Obstetrics and Gynecology
Recommendations: 1) Secure two large-bore intravenous catheters (16-gauge or larger) and initiate crystalloid resuscitation. 2) Prepare for rapid sequence induction general anesthesia using modified technique (propofol or etomidate, succinylcholine or rocuronium); note that magnesium sulfate potentiates nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents—reduce rocuronium dose and prepare for prolonged blockade. 3) Have vasopressors (phenylephrine, ephedrine, norepinephrine) immediately available for severe hypertension management and potential post-induction hypotension. 4) Activate massive transfusion protocol; ensure availability of packed red blood cells, fresh frozen plasma, platelets, and cryoprecipitate given thrombocytopenia and risk of DIC. 5) Continue magnesium sulfate infusion perioperatively for seizure prophylaxis. 6) Anticipate uterine atony; have oxytocin, methergine, carboprost, and misoprostol ready. 7) Consider arterial line placement for continuous BP monitoring given severe hypertension and risk of hemodynamic lability. 8) Prepare for potential intensive care unit admission postoperatively for ongoing monitoring of coagulopathy, renal function, and neurologic status. 9) Notify neonatology team for anticipated neonatal resuscitation given fetal distress and prematurity.
Notes: Platelet count may continue to decline rapidly in HELLP syndrome; repeat platelet count immediately before incision if any delay occurs. Neuraxial anesthesia is relatively contraindicated given thrombocytopenia and risk of epidural hematoma. Avoid NSAIDs postoperatively given platelet count and renal dysfunction.

winner_protocol:
Age: 34
Sex: Woman
Complaint: 12-day history of productive cough with diffuse wheezes on lung auscultation, preceded by nasal congestion and sore throat.
Analysis: The clinical picture is most consistent with acute bronchitis complicated by transient bronchial hyperreactivity. Key supporting facts include: (1) an antecedent upper respiratory illness (nasal congestion, sore throat) that has since resolved; (2) no known underlying lung disease and no prior wheezing episodes mentioned; (3) afebrile, normal vital signs, no respiratory distress; (4) productive cough without paroxysms; (5) diffuse scattered wheezes on auscultation. The main differential consideration is newly unmasked or underlying asthma. The absence of a prior wheezing history and the clear temporal relationship to a viral URI favor acute bronchitis-related bronchospasm over asthma. Response to a bronchodilator trial would help confirm transient hyperreactivity. Persistent wheeze after resolution of the acute illness would warrant further evaluation for asthma.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Stethoscope (already performed). A trial of an inhaled short-acting bronchodilator to assess clinical response. Spirometry is not needed at this stage but should be considered if wheeze persists after the acute illness resolves.
Conclusion: Acute bronchitis with transient bronchial hyperreactivity presenting as diffuse wheezing following a viral upper respiratory illness. No evidence of pneumonia or respiratory compromise. Underlying asthma cannot be fully excluded but is less likely given no prior wheezing history.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology

winner_protocol:
Age: 24-year-old
Sex: Male
Complaint: Painful small bump in the beard area appearing 2 days after shaving with a multi-blade razor against the grain.
Analysis: The clinical picture is most consistent with pseudofolliculitis barbae (ingrown hair). Key supporting findings include: (1) onset 2 days after shaving with a multi-blade razor used against the grain—a known risk factor; (2) a single erythematous, firm 4 mm papule in the submandibular/beard area; (3) a curled hair visible beneath the skin surface, which is pathognomonic for an ingrown hair. Differential considerations: bacterial folliculitis is less likely given the absence of a pustule, drainage, or fever; furuncle is ruled out by the absence of fluctuance, induration, and purulent drainage; epidermoid cyst is unlikely given the acute post-shaving onset and visible curled hair; acne keloidalis nuchae typically occurs at the nape of the neck rather than the submandibular area. Red flags screened and absent: patient denies fever, spreading redness, and drainage; examination confirms no fluctuance, induration, or streaking erythema. No history of recurrent skin infections.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None — diagnosis is clinical based on history and physical examination.
Conclusion: Uncomplicated pseudofolliculitis barbae (ingrown hair) of the right submandibular area, without evidence of secondary bacterial infection or abscess formation.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: 1) Apply warm compresses to the lesion for 10–15 minutes, 2–3 times daily, to reduce inflammation and encourage the hair to surface. 2) If the curled hair tip is easily accessible, use a sterile needle or clean tweezers to gently lift the hair above the skin; do not dig into the skin or pluck the hair from the root. 2) Avoid shaving the affected area until the lesion has fully healed. 3) For future shaving: shave with the grain rather than against it; consider switching from a multi-blade razor to a single-blade safety razor or electric trimmer; use a moisturizing shaving gel or cream; avoid stretching the skin taut while shaving; shave after showering when hairs are softened. 4) Consider an over-the-counter topical benzoyl peroxide 5% wash or mild topical hydrocortisone 1% for a few days to reduce inflammation. 5) Return promptly if the lesion develops increasing pain, spreading redness, pus, fever, or enlarging swelling, which may indicate secondary infection requiring antibiotics or drainage.
Notes: Recurrent or persistent pseudofolliculitis barbae despite technique modification may warrant dermatology referral for consideration of longer-term management strategies such as laser hair removal.

The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.

- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case

criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.

Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.

Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.

- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.

winner_protocol:
Age: 56
Sex: Female
Complaint: Persistent poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus with rising HbA1c (7.6% to 8.1%) despite maximal oral therapy (metformin 1000 mg BID, glimepiride 8 mg daily), accompanied by polyuria, polydipsia, and diabetic peripheral neuropathy; patient previously refused insulin due to fear of needles.
Analysis: This patient has type 2 diabetes that has worsened despite escalation of sulfonylurea therapy to maximum dose and reported adherence to metformin, diet, and exercise. Her HbA1c has risen from 7.6% to 8.1% over 3 months, and she now has symptomatic hyperglycemia (increased thirst and urination). She has developed peripheral neuropathy (numbness/tingling in feet, decreased sensation on exam) and exhibits acanthosis nigricans, confirming significant insulin resistance. Her oral medication regimen has been maximized—metformin at maximum dose and glimepiride at maximum dose—yet glycemic control is deteriorating. The primary barrier to insulin initiation is her fear of needles, which was explicitly documented at the prior visit. Key differential considerations include: (1) genuine need for therapy escalation beyond oral agents, as evidenced by worsening A1c despite maximal oral therapy and reported adherence; (2) possible dietary non-adherence not fully captured by self-report, given her diet includes pizza and pasta; (3) inadequate physical activity (only 1–2 days/week, 20 minutes). Her blood pressure is also poorly controlled at 159/88 mmHg despite lisinopril 40 mg, requiring attention. The strongest supporting facts for therapy escalation are: A1c progression on maximal oral therapy, symptomatic hyperglycemia, stable weight (arguing against overt non-adherence causing weight changes), and objective neuropathy on examination.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Lipid panel (currently pending—needed to assess cardiovascular risk and statin adequacy); comprehensive foot examination with monofilament testing (to formally stage neuropathy); urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (to screen for diabetic nephropathy given long-standing diabetes and hypertension).
Conclusion: A 56-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and obesity whose glycemic control has deteriorated (HbA1c 8.1%) despite maximal oral therapy. She has symptomatic hyperglycemia, early diabetic peripheral neuropathy, acanthosis nigricans, and poorly controlled hypertension. Her fear of needles remains a significant barrier to insulin therapy. Oral medication options have been exhausted, and injectable therapy is clinically indicated. A stepwise approach addressing her needle phobia while introducing non-insulin injectable or additional oral agents is warranted, with endocrinology referral if control does not improve.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology
Recommendations: 1) Initiate a GLP-1 receptor agonist (e.g., weekly subcutaneous semaglutide or dulaglutide) as the preferred next-line agent—this addresses hyperglycemia, promotes weight loss (beneficial given BMI 34.9), and once-weekly dosing with a small pen needle may be more acceptable to a patient with needle phobia than daily insulin. Frame the needle as very fine and weekly rather than daily to reduce psychological barrier. 2) Alternatively or additionally, add an SGLT-2 inhibitor (e.g., empagliflozin) as an oral agent that does not require injection, provides modest A1c reduction, and offers cardiovascular and renal benefits. 3) Continue metformin 1000 mg BID; consider reducing or discontinuing glimepiride given risk of hypoglycemia with combination therapy and its limited additional benefit at maximum dose. 4) Address hypertension: add amlodipine 5–10 mg daily or a thiazide diuretic to lisinopril 40 mg to achieve BP target <130/80 mmHg. 5) Reinforce dietary counseling—specifically reduce refined carbohydrates (pizza, pasta) and increase frequency of physical activity toward 150 minutes/week of moderate exercise. 6) Refer to diabetes self-management education and support program. 7) Refer to endocrinology for consideration of insulin therapy if A1c does not improve within 3 months, with continued counseling on needle phobia. 8) Schedule follow-up in 4–6 weeks to assess tolerance of new therapy, repeat fingerstick glucose, and recheck blood pressure. 9) Review lipid panel when results return and adjust statin therapy if needed. 10) Perform annual diabetic eye examination and ensure foot care education given confirmed neuropathy.
Notes: Patient's fear of needles should be addressed with empathy and specific strategies (e.g., insulin pen needles as fine as 32-gauge, use of GLP-1 agonist with weekly dosing, potential referral to behavioral health for phobia management). Do not discontinue glimepiride abruptly without alternative coverage. Monitor for hypoglycemia if GLP-1 agonist or SGLT-2 inhibitor is added to sulfonylurea. SGLT-2 inhibitors carry risk of genital mycotic infections—counsel patient accordingly. Lipid panel results are pending and must be reviewed before finalizing cardiovascular risk management.

Diagnosis10cm: Left tubal pregnancy without intrauterine pregnancy
Vignette: A 28-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of severe left-sided pelvic pain and lightheadedness that began 45 minutes ago. She reports 7 weeks of amenorrhea and a positive home pregnancy test 5 days ago. She has a history of pelvic inflammatory disease and a prior left tubal ectopic pregnancy treated with methotrexate 2 years ago. On examination, she is pale, diaphoretic, and appears acutely ill. Vital signs: T 36.4C, HR 132, RR 24, BP 78/48, SpO2 97%. Abdominal exam reveals diffuse lower abdominal tenderness with peritoneal signs. Hemoglobin returns at 7.8 g/dL. O-negative blood is ordered and the OR is alerted for emergent laparotomy.

Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.

It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.

Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.

Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.

Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. - the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
